d: Stacks are data structures that follow the Last in First Out (LIFO) principle.
h:
A stack is a linear data structure with a collection of items that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle. The top of the stack is the item most recently added to the stack, and the bottom of the stack is the item that was least recently added.

You can think of the stack data structure as a stack of dinner plates: you start with one, and then you put another above it. When you take plates from the stack, the first one you remove from the stack is the last one you put on the top.

Stacks have two main operations: push for adding an element to the top of the stack and pop for removing the element from the top of the stack. A Stack can either have a fixed size or be dynamically resized. Stacks are helpful for design usage such as backtracking algorithms.

Implement stacks

Though Luau doesn't have stacks as a built-in data structure, you can use tables to implement stacks. The following code sample shows how to create a stack, push an object to a stack, and pop an object from the stack. To use this implementation for your game, you should save it as a ModuleScript and store it in ReplicatedStorage, so your stack is accessible for both client and server.

local Stack = {}
Stack.__index = Stack

function Stack.new()
    local self = setmetatable({}, Stack)

    self._stack = {}

    return self
end

-- Check if the stack is empty
function Stack:isEmpty()
    return #self._stack == 0
end

-- Put a new value onto the stack
function Stack:push(value)
    table.insert(self._stack, value)
end

-- Take a value off the stack
function Stack:pop()
    if self:isEmpty() then
        return nil
    end

    return table.remove(self._stack, #self._stack)
end

return Stack

The following code sample is a usage example as a Script under Workspace. You can modify the code, type, and storage location to fit your own usage, as long as you have the previous implementation code sample properly stored.

Stack Usage Example

local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Stack = require(ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Stack"))

local s = Stack.new()

-- Change the stack     Resulting stack      Output

s:push(1)               -- {1}

s:push(5)               -- {1, 5}

s:push(10)              -- {1, 5, 10}

print(s:pop())          -- {1, 5}            10

print(s:pop())          -- {1}               5

s:push(20)              -- {1, 20}

print(s:pop())          -- {1}               20

print(s:pop())          -- {}                1

When running pop() on a stack, make sure the stack is not empty.

If you run the previous code sample without changing anything, the expected output is:

Example Output

10
5
20
1

kid.simple: A stack is a pile of items where the last one you put on is the first one you take off. That is called Last In, First Out, or LIFO. Stacks are handy for things like an undo button or going back through menus. Luau does not have stacks built in, but a table makes a great one.
kid.analogy: A stack is like a pile of dinner plates. You put new plates on top, and when you grab one, you take the top plate, which is the last one you added.
keyPoints: A stack follows LIFO: last in, first out.
The top is the newest item; the bottom is the oldest.
Push means add an item to the top. Pop means remove the item from the top.
Stacks help with backtracking, like undo or going back to the previous screen.
You can build a stack with a table using `table.insert` to push and `table.remove` to pop.
Always make sure the stack is not empty before you pop.
The page suggests saving the stack code as a ModuleScript in ReplicatedStorage so both server and client can use it.

terms.stack: A list where you only add and remove at the top.
terms.LIFO: Last In, First Out. The last item added is the first one removed.
terms.push: To add an item to the top of the stack.
terms.pop: To remove and return the item on top of the stack.
terms.top / bottom: The top is the most recently added item; the bottom is the one added longest ago.
terms.backtracking: Going back step by step through what you did before, like pressing undo several times.
terms.dynamically resized: Able to grow or shrink as you add or remove items.

example.title: Undo for a building game
example.code:
local history = {} -- our stack

local function push(action)
	table.insert(history, action) -- add to the top
end

local function pop()
	if #history == 0 then
		return nil -- nothing to undo
	end
	return table.remove(history, #history) -- take from the top
end

push("Placed red block")
push("Placed blue block")
push("Painted wall")

print("Undo:", pop()) --> Undo: Painted wall
print("Undo:", pop()) --> Undo: Placed blue block
push("Placed door")
print("Undo:", pop()) --> Undo: Placed door
print("Undo:", pop()) --> Undo: Placed red block
print("Undo:", pop()) --> Undo: nil
explain: `history` is a table used as a stack.
`push` adds each action to the end of the table, which is the top of the stack.
`pop` removes and returns the last item, so the newest action is undone first.
If the stack is empty, `pop` returns `nil` instead of causing a problem.

watchOut: Popping an empty stack. Check `#history == 0` first.
Using `table.remove(history, 1)`. That takes from the bottom, which makes it act like a queue, not a stack.
